data.targetWord: The belief that violence and war are never justifiable under any circumstances — a principled commitment to non-violence

examples.en-GB: Gandhi's pacifism shaped the Indian independence movement through non-violent resistance rather than armed revolt.

data.targetWord: A theory holding that war may sometimes be morally justified if it meets specific criteria, such as having a just cause, being a last resort, and protecting civilians

examples.en-GB: Just war theory was developed by Christian thinkers including Augustine and Aquinas to address when, if ever, war is permissible.

data.targetWord: The process of restoring a broken relationship or rebuilding trust after conflict, harm, or wrongdoing

examples.en-GB: Archbishop Desmond Tutu's work on reconciliation in post-apartheid South Africa showed how acknowledgement and forgiveness can rebuild a society.

data.targetWord: A person who refuses to serve in the military or to participate in war on grounds of religious or moral belief

examples.en-GB: Conscientious objectors in World War I often served as medical orderlies, showing courage without combat.

data.targetWord: A just war principle requiring that the force used in a conflict must not exceed what is necessary to achieve a just aim — no excessive destruction

examples.en-GB: Proportionality forbids destroying an entire city in response to an attack on a small military target.

data.targetWord: A just war criterion requiring that all peaceful alternatives — diplomacy, negotiation, sanctions — must have been exhausted before force is used

examples.en-GB: A war that begins before diplomatic options are fully explored fails the 'last resort' criterion of just war theory.

data.targetWord: A just war criterion requiring that a war is fought to defend against attack or prevent serious injustice — not for territory, profit, or revenge

examples.en-GB: Defending a nation that has been invaded without provocation is generally considered a just cause.

data.targetWord: The use of violence against civilians to create fear and advance political aims — condemned by all major world religions

examples.en-GB: Terrorism is not representative of any religion; every major faith explicitly condemns the targeting of innocent civilians.

data.targetWord: Releasing resentment and choosing not to seek revenge against someone who has caused harm — distinct from excusing or condoning the harm

examples.en-GB: Forgiveness does not mean the wrongdoer faces no consequences — it means the victim frees themselves from destructive hatred.

data.targetWord: The process of helping parties in conflict reach an agreement through a neutral third party who does not take sides

examples.en-GB: Religious leaders often serve as trusted mediators in community conflicts because they are respected by different groups.

data.targetWord: The Sikh concept of the 'saint-soldier' — a Sikh should be peaceful and devout but willing to defend the oppressed with force if necessary

examples.en-GB: The Sant Sipahi ideal explains why the kirpan is worn — as a symbol of the duty to defend justice.

data.targetWord: The Sikh concept of 'righteous war' — the Sikh equivalent of just war theory, permitting the use of force to defend justice and protect the oppressed

examples.en-GB: Dharam yudh means that for Sikhs, violence used to defend the innocent against oppression can be morally justified.

data.targetWord: Gandhi's concept of 'truth-force' or 'soul-force' — the principle that non-violent resistance, grounded in truth and love, is stronger than armed force

examples.en-GB: Gandhi used satyagraha — non-violent resistance — as the foundation of the Indian independence campaign against British rule.

data.targetWord: An African philosophical concept meaning 'I am because we are' — human dignity is shared and interconnected, used by Archbishop Tutu in reconciliation theology

examples.en-GB: Archbishop Tutu's Ubuntu theology held that you cannot truly flourish while others are oppressed — justice and peace are inseparable.

data.targetWord: A Christian reconciliation community in Northern Ireland that worked across community divisions during and after the Troubles to build peace

examples.en-GB: Corrymeela brought together Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland to rebuild relationships across the sectarian divide.

data.targetWord: The movement, associated with Thich Nhat Hanh, that applies Buddhist principles of compassion and non-violence to social, political, and environmental issues

examples.en-GB: Thich Nhat Hanh coined the term 'engaged Buddhism' to describe his peace activism during the Vietnam War.

data.targetWord: Striking back in response to an attack — revenge — which may escalate conflict rather than resolve it

examples.en-GB: Many religious traditions warn against retaliation, arguing that it perpetuates cycles of violence.

data.targetWord: The refusal to use physical force to resolve disputes — a positive commitment to peaceful means of change rather than merely the absence of violence

examples.en-GB: Martin Luther King Jr. used non-violence not as weakness but as a powerful moral force in the civil rights movement.

data.targetWord: Holding and acting on extreme views — including the belief that violence is justified to achieve political or ideological goals — often misusing religious language

examples.en-GB: Extremists who claim religious justification for terrorism distort and misuse their tradition's teachings.

data.targetWord: Compassion and leniency towards an opponent, enemy, or wrongdoer rather than the maximum punishment — treating people with humanity even in conflict

examples.en-GB: Showing mercy to a defeated enemy is compatible with justice and is encouraged by many religious traditions.

data.sentence: The belief that violence and war are never justifiable under any circumstances is called ____.

The just war criterion that war must only be fought when all peaceful alternatives have failed is called ____.
The just war principle that a military response must not use more force than is necessary is called ____.
Restoring a broken relationship or rebuilding trust after conflict is called ____.
A person who refuses to fight in war on grounds of religious or moral belief is called a ____ objector.
The Sikh concept of the 'saint-soldier' — devout but willing to defend the oppressed — is called ____ Sipahi.
Gandhi called his principle of non-violent resistance grounded in truth '____ ' — meaning truth-force or soul-force.
The use of violence against civilians to create fear and advance political aims is called ____.
Releasing resentment and choosing not to seek revenge is called ____.
Archbishop Tutu's concept of ____ — 'I am because we are' — held that human dignity is shared and interconnected.
The Christian reconciliation centre in Northern Ireland that worked across community divisions during the Troubles is called ____.
The Sikh concept of righteous or justified war — the Sikh equivalent of just war theory — is called ____ yudh.
Helping parties in conflict reach an agreement through a neutral third party is called ____.
Just war theory requires that a war has a ____ cause — it must be fought to defend against attack or prevent serious injustice, not for territory or revenge.

data.title: Put the stages of a reconciliation process in the correct order, from harm occurring to trust being rebuilt.
items: Harm occurs — a wrong is committed
Acknowledgement — the harm is named and the wrongdoer admits what happened
Apology — a genuine expression of remorse
Forgiveness — the victim releases resentment and reconciliation begins

data.title: Put these just war criteria in a logical order when evaluating whether a proposed war is justified.
items: Check that there is a just cause — defending against attack or preventing serious injustice
Verify that proper authority has declared the war
Confirm that all peaceful alternatives have been exhausted (last resort)
Assess whether the intended response is proportionate to the threat
Ensure that civilians can be protected from targeting

data.title: Put these peace-building actions in order from immediate response to long-term change.
items: Provide emergency aid and protection to those caught in conflict
Begin ceasefire negotiations with mediation from trusted third parties
Establish a truth and reconciliation process to acknowledge past harm
Rebuild community relationships through interfaith dialogue and shared projects
Create education programmes to prevent future prejudice and promote mutual understanding
